## The question

Boykoff & Boykoff
([GLOBAL ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGE, 2004](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2003.10.001))
read the climate coverage of four US newspapers from 1988 to 2002 by hand.
About half the stories gave equal space to the scientists who said people
are warming the planet and to those who doubted it. How often did New York
Times climate stories state warming, or its human cause, as uncertain from
1988 to 2026? Here you will use a large language model with open weights
on your own laptop to read these stories and make a similar
classification.

## What counts as uncertain

Only the warming itself, or people's role in causing it, counts. Some
made-up sentences and how to label them:

| Sentence | Label |
|:--|:--|
| Scientists predict that burning coal and oil may warm the planet. | uncertain |
| Whether people are changing the climate is still in dispute. | uncertain |
| The planet has warmed about 1 degree Celsius in a century, mostly from burning fossil fuels. | fact |
| Warming could cut wheat yields by a tenth, though estimates vary. | fact: the doubt is about an effect |
| Some senators doubt that people cause warming; most climate scientists say the evidence is clear. | fact: the story reports the doubt and states the science as settled |
| Delegates argued late into the night over emission targets. | not stated |

## Data

1. **The New York Times: an API.** The Archive API returns everything the
   paper published in one month as JSON: headline, summary, first
   paragraph, date, type, subject tags and address. There is no article
   text.
   `https://api.nytimes.com/svc/archive/v1/1988/6.json?api-key=...`
   It needs a free key: create an account at
   <https://developer.nytimes.com>, add an app, and enable the Archive API
   for it. The API allows 500 requests a day, 12 seconds apart, so the 466
   months from January 1988 to October 2026 take about two and a half
   hours.
2. **Global temperature: a CSV.** NASA GISTEMP v4, one row a year, the
   annual mean in column `J-D`:
   <https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/tabledata_v4/GLB.Ts+dSST.csv>
3. **The model: open weights, on your laptop.** `qwen3.5:9b-q4_K_M`, run
   through Ollama. Setup is below.

A month holds 4,000 to 10,000 items. Keep the climate items and the fields
you use, save each month, and never request a month twice.

## How long it took me

On my laptop (a MacBook Pro with an M2 Max chip and 64 GB of memory), the
466 downloads took about two and a half hours and the model close to three
hours: about 2,900 topic calls and 2,000 hedging calls, close to 2 seconds
each. A laptop without an Apple chip or a graphics card can be several
times slower. Time the model on 20 stories, then plan the full run,
overnight if you need to. Save every reply, so a run that stops picks up
where it stopped. Start early.

## The model

1. Install Ollama from <https://ollama.com/download> (Mac, Windows or
   Linux) and open it. It runs in the background and serves the model on
   your laptop.
2. In the Terminal, download the model once (6.6 GB):
   `ollama pull qwen3.5:9b-q4_K_M`. On a laptop with 8 GB of memory or
   less, use `qwen3.5:4b-q4_K_M` (3.3 GB) instead and say so in
   `NOTES.md`.
3. Check that it answers: `ollama run qwen3.5:9b-q4_K_M "Say hello"`.
4. In R, install `ellmer` and call the model with `chat_ollama()`. In
   `params()`, set the temperature to 0, the seed to 6850, and
   `reasoning_effort = "none"` to turn its thinking off. With thinking on,
   each call takes much longer.

## Your key

Save it in `~/.Renviron` as `NYT_KEY=...`, restart R, and read it with
`Sys.getenv("NYT_KEY")`. The key must never appear in your code, your
notes or a commit. GitHub keeps every commit, so a key deleted later is
still in the history; if one reaches GitHub, delete it at
developer.nytimes.com and make a new one.

## Which stories

- **Tagged stories** carry one of the paper's subject tags: Global
  Warming, Greenhouse Effect, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, or United Nations
  Framework Convention on Climate Change. The tags are in `keywords`,
  where `name` is `subject`; older items have them in capitals.
- **News stories only:** `type_of_material` is `News`. Drop blog posts,
  whose address contains `blogs.nytimes.com` or `/blogs/` (some years type
  them as News), and stories that appear twice.
- **At most 100 stories a year**, drawn at random from that year's
  tagged stories after `set.seed(6850)`, so the model's work stays near
  three hours. Every year before 2006 has fewer than 100, so all of them
  are read. That is about 2,900 of the 10,275 stories. You may have the
  model read every story; on a laptop that takes about three times as
  long.

## The labels

Ask the model two questions about each story's headline, summary and first
paragraph, one call each, without the date:

1. Is the story's main subject climate change? This is a second filter:
   the tags also catch stories that only touch on climate.
2. For the stories that are: does it state that the Earth is warming, or
   that people are causing it, as fact or as uncertain, or does it say
   nothing about it? Only the warming and its cause count. Doubt about the
   effects, the costs or a treaty does not.

Asking the model to copy the words about warming before it answers helps.
Write each prompt like the codebook in session 17: one sentence on what
the model reads, one line defining each label, with the words that signal
uncertainty (predict, believe, may, could, theory), then rules for the
cases in between, including what does not count. My climate-filter
prompt has 3 sentences (about 75 words) and my hedging prompt 10 (about
180). Label at least 30 stories yourself before you look at the
model's answers, and compare. Change one thing in the prompt at a time,
and check each version against your hand labels.

## Output

- `figures/hw4_target.png`, 10 × 10.5 inches at 200 dpi.
- `data_clean/labels.csv`: one row per story the model read, with its id,
  date and both answers.
- `data_clean/stories_per_year.csv`: the tagged news stories each year.
- `NOTES.md`: the number of stories left after each filter, your two
  questions word for word, your hand check (how many stories, how many the
  model got right, and the ones it got wrong), and an AI disclosure (tools,
  uses, what you checked).

## Figure rules

- Three panels stacked on one time axis, 1988 to 2026. Mark 2026 with a
  star: it runs to October.
- Top: climate stories per year, the tagged news stories times the share
  the model found to be about climate change. An arrow and a label mark
  five events: the UN climate conferences in Kyoto (COP3, 1997),
  Copenhagen (COP15, 2009), Paris (COP21, 2015) and Glasgow (COP26, 2021),
  and the IPCC's Fourth Assessment Report (AR4, 2007).
- Middle: each year's share of climate stories that state warming, or its
  human cause, as uncertain, one bar a year.
- Bottom: one cell a year, coloured by global temperature from cool to
  warm.
- A dark background.

Font, exact shades and the key's layout are never differences. Your bars
may not match the target image exactly: the stories in your sample, the
wording of your two questions and the model you use all move them a
little.

## How to submit

Your repository is **`hw4-<your github username>`** in the course
organization. It holds only a README that links to this page; the
project's layout is yours to set up. Put the code in `code/`, with
`code/run_everything.R` running it all, and paths relative to the project
root. Do not commit the months you download, since the paper's terms do
not allow sharing them: list that folder in `.gitignore`. Commit the two
CSV files above instead. The grader has no NYT key, so the script that
draws the figure must run from a fresh clone with those two files and
NASA's CSV. Commit as you go; the grader uses the last commit pushed
before the deadline.
